intended_object: Orthogonality of two classes of morphisms L ⊥ R in a category: every l ∈ L is (uniquely-lifting) orthogonal to every r ∈ R, i.e. every commuting square with l on the left and r on the right has a unique diagonal filler. Inferred from the comment "The predicate of classes of morphisms being orthogonal", the name, and the factorization-systems context.
explanation: The body says that `orthogonal l r` holds for all l with L l and all r with R r. `orthogonal` (in Orthogonality.lean) gives a diagonal filler for every commuting square `l □ r` (a map B ⟶ X with l ≫ d = top and d ≫ r = bot), together with a proof that any two fillers have the same map. That is existence plus uniqueness of lifts, the standard notion of orthogonality used for orthogonal factorization systems. `orthogonal` is a data-carrying structure, but because fillers are unique it has at most one element, so `orthogonalClass` behaves like the intended proposition. The definition is stated for an arbitrary category and arbitrary morphism classes, which is the natural generality. Mathlib has no unique-lifting orthogonality of morphism classes: `HasLiftingProperty` and `MorphismProperty.llp`/`rlp` only require a lift to exist, so they describe the weak notion.
